Number
NUM-ber
n., v.
Middle English nombre, from Old French, from Latin numerus — a count, sum, quantity. Related to Greek nomos (law, allotment) and to nemein (to distribute, assign). In Hebrew, saphar (to count, recount, declare) is also the root of sepher (scroll, book): to count is already to tell, to record, to make known.

Biblical Definition

In Scripture, number is never merely arithmetic — it is the language of divine accounting. God numbers the stars and calls them all by name (Isa 40:26; Ps 147:4); He numbers the hairs of every head (Luke 12:7; Matt 10:30); He numbers the days of His saints and commands them to number their own (Ps 90:12). This is not the counting of an indifferent calculator but the caring enumeration of a Father who knows and names every unit of His creation. The great multitude of Revelation 7:9 — from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue — is explicitly a company “that no one could number”: the only uncountable thing in the universe is the redeemed in glory, precisely because God’s electing grace exceeds every human tally. Israel was numbered twice in the wilderness (the book of Numbers takes its name from the two censuses); those numbers were not administrative data but the covenant register of God’s army, each name a testimony to God’s faithfulness to the promises made to Abraham. To “number our days” (Ps 90:12) is to practice creaturely realism under the sovereignty of the God who appoints every day: not a morbid arithmetic but the path to wisdom, for only the creature who knows its own finitude walks humbly before the infinite God. Scripture concludes with a number that demands wisdom to calculate (Rev 13:18) — 666, the number of the beast. Number in Scripture, from the census of Israel to the number of the stars, is always an act of divine knowledge and covenant care.

Webster 1828 Definition

A word or symbol expressing quantity; in Scripture, the instrument of divine knowledge and covenant care — God who numbers stars, hairs, and days; the great multitude no one can number in glory; and the beast’s number that demands wisdom.

expand to see more

NUMBER, n. & v. That which expresses how many; a unit of the divine ledger. Webster (1828) defined number as ‘that by which things are counted or reckoned.’ Scripture employs it as an act of covenant accountability: every soul is numbered, every hair counted, every day appointed, every nation enrolled in the Lamb’s book of life.

As a verb, ‘to number’ in Scripture always implies knowing and caring: God numbers the stars (Isa 40:26) not to satisfy cosmic curiosity but to demonstrate that He who created and named them sustains them by His might. To command His people to ‘number our days’ (Ps 90:12) is to prescribe the medicine of creaturely finitude as the path to wisdom.

Key Scripture

Psalm 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Revelation 7:9 — "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;"

Luke 12:7 — "But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows."

Isaiah 40:26 — "Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth."

Modern Corruption

Secular culture treats number as a neutral, self-interpreting tool of data science, stripping it of its Creator’s personal knowledge; occult numerology invests number with inherent magical power, making it a source of divination rather than a servant of divine accounting.

expand to see more

Modern data culture presupposes that number is a neutral tool: everything important can be measured, quantified, and managed by the right metric. This is a form of idolatry — the reduction of persons to data points, of communities to statistics, of creaturely life to manipulable quantities. Scripture counters: the God who numbers the hairs of every head is not calculating an aggregate. He knows names, not only counts. Every number in the divine ledger is a person with a face.

Occult numerology inverts the biblical pattern by treating number as an inherent power: the number itself, apart from the God who counts, possesses and confers meaning, luck, fate, or spiritual force. This severs number from the Personal God who alone assigns significance. The Bible’s numbered census, its numbered days, and its numbered remnant all point beyond themselves to the One who counts — removing Him leaves an empty symbol dressed in the appearance of cosmic order.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew root saphar links number with narrative (scroll, declaration) from the beginning, insisting that to count is also to tell — the universe is not merely enumerable but storied, and every number belongs to a story the Creator is writing.

expand to see more

Latin numerus — number, count; source of “numeral,” “numerous,” “enumerate.”

Hebrew saphar — to count, declare, recount; root of both mispar (number) and sepher (scroll, book).

Greek arithmos — number; used in “arithmetic” and in Rev 13:18 (“the number of a man”).

Greek nomos / nemein — to assign, distribute; shares a root with numerus, linking number to law and allotment.

Old French nombre — ancestor of English “number” via medieval French transmission.

Usage

"To number our days is not a morbid arithmetic but the beginning of wisdom: only the creature who honestly reckons its own finitude walks humbly before the Infinite."

"The great multitude no one could number (Rev 7:9) is the single uncountable thing in all of Scripture — not because God does not know them but because their fullness exceeds every human census."

"God’s numbering of the hairs of our head is not a statement about divine trivia management; it is a statement about the quality of His personal, particularizing knowledge of every creature He loves."
